title: Can Workers Predict Job Finding and Job Loss? - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed researchers compare SCE worker expectations with realized CPS flows: job-finding expectations tracked reality pre-COVID (55.5% vs 57.2%) but since 2022 workers are persistently pessimistic (53.0% expected vs 58.8% realized), driven by under-30 and non-college workers. Expected job-loss risk runs about double realized, especially for long-tenured workers who underestimate how much tenure protects them.

insights.claim: Before COVID, workers' expected 3-month job-finding rate in the NY Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations (55.5% avg 2014-2019) closely matched the realized CPS rate for newly unemployed workers (57.2%).
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Establishes the SCE job-finding expectation as a historically well-calibrated labor gauge, so post-2020 deviations are signal, not noise.

insights.claim: Since 2022, the realized 3-month job-finding rate for newly unemployed US workers has averaged 58.8% while SCE expected job-finding probabilities have fallen to 53.0%, a persistent pessimistic wedge of roughly 6 points.
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Survey-based labor sentiment currently understates actual labor-market strength; don't read weak SCE job-finding expectations as a pure deterioration signal.
insights.quote: workers have been persistently pessimistic about their chances of finding a job in the post-pandemic period

insights.claim: Actual US job-finding rates recovered to pre-COVID levels by 2021, but workers' job-finding expectations stayed subdued far longer, showing expectations lag reality on the way back up.
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Sentiment indicators may lag labor recoveries; consumer caution (precautionary saving) can persist after fundamentals heal.

insights.claim: Workers did not anticipate COVID: the true three-month-ahead job-finding rate dropped steeply at end-2019 while expectations only fell at the pandemic onset in March 2020, so worker expectations are reactive rather than predictive of shocks.
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Don't rely on household labor expectations as a leading indicator of exogenous shocks; they move with, not ahead of, the event.

themes.theme: Young and non-college workers turned pessimistic

insights.claim: The post-COVID decline in job-finding expectations relative to realized rates is driven primarily by workers aged 30 or younger and those without college degrees.
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Watch youth and non-college sentiment separately; aggregate labor sentiment weakness is concentrated in these cohorts.
insights.locator: The post-COVID decline in job-finding expectations

insights.claim: Workers aged 30 or younger flipped from optimism before COVID (expected job-finding 6.3 pp above realized) to pessimism after (3.0 pp below realized), a swing of over 9 percentage points.
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Young-worker sentiment shifted most; relevant for spending, household formation and consumer discretionary exposure to younger cohorts.
insights.locator: However, those aged 30 or younger shifted

insights.claim: Workers with a high school degree or less had job-finding expectations roughly aligned with reality before COVID, but post-2020 they underestimate by 7.5 percentage points, the largest negative gap of any group.
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Lower-education workers' excess pessimism could depress their spending and search intensity beyond what labor data justify.
insights.locator: Before COVID, workers with a high school degree

insights.claim: Workers over 30 and those with some college were already pessimistic before COVID (underestimating job-finding by about 5.4 and 4.6 pp) and their gaps barely changed after the pandemic (6.1 and 4.0 pp).
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Baseline pessimism among older/educated workers is structural, so changes in their sentiment are less informative than shifts among young/non-college cohorts.

insights.claim: Overly negative perceptions among new labor-market entrants may themselves contribute to the downbeat youth labor-market outlook, alongside higher post-pandemic youth unemployment.
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Youth labor weakness may be partly a perception problem; narrative-driven pessimism can feed reduced search or acceptance behavior.

insights.claim: US workers' expected job-loss probability (SCE, converted to a 3-month horizon) is about twice the realized CPS employment-to-unemployment rate, consistently over time since 2013.
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Household layoff fears run structurally hot; elevated SCE job-loss expectations should be judged against this persistent upward bias.

insights.claim: The gap between expected and realized job loss is not necessarily excess pessimism, because the CPS measure misses job losses followed by labor-force exit and quits ahead of layoffs, making it a lower bound on job-loss risk.
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Treat the job-loss gap as partly measurement artifact; the job-finding gap is the cleaner sentiment signal.
insights.quote: Our measure should therefore be viewed as a lower bound of job-loss risk.
insights.locator: This gap does not necessarily imply excessive pessimism

insights.claim: Realized job-loss rates fall steadily as tenure at the current job rises, but perceived job-loss risk declines much less sharply, so workers underestimate the job security that comes with longer tenure.
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: Long-tenured workers likely hold excess precautionary savings relative to true risk; layoff-fear surveys overstate risk for the established workforce.

insights.claim: After two years on the job, workers' expected probability of job loss is more than twice the realized rate, and the expected-vs-realized gap widens with tenure.
insights.speaker: Richard Audoly
insights.so_what: The overstatement of layoff risk is largest among established workers, the bulk of consumer spending power.
